newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Fresh trouble in Albania as police disrupt rally.
newsitem.headline: Fresh trouble in Albania as police disrupt rally.

text.p: Albanian police punched and jostled demonstrators on Wednesday to break up an anti-government rally called by one of the leaders of a 1990 revolt which toppled the former communist regime.

Witnesses saw 40 to 50 police officers pushing a small crowd of around 200 people who had gathered to support former student leader Hazem Hajdari's call on the government to sort out a savings scheme crisis.
But Hajdari had no chance to address the crowd as police became more aggressive, shouting abuse and heaving people off a soccer field where they had gathered, punching the most reluctant to move.
A small number of officers used rubber truncheons but there was little of the violence seen in central Tirana last Sunday when riot police and protesters clashed.
"Look at them, and they call this a democracy," one woman shouted as police vans sped on streets around the soccer stadium.
There were reports that students were prevented from reaching the stadium after police blocked roads around their campus.
A group of women set upon police officers to stop them dragging one man into a police van. At least three people were arrested.

Many of those in the field were investors who had put money in a failed pyramid investment scheme. Albania has been hit by a wave of violence over the past three weeks since the investment scams began to crumble, leaving thousands penniless.
"The protests will go on. We will protest in a civilised way to defend the economic and social interests of the workers," Hajdari told reporters.
A comprehensive solution had to be found to the savings collapse and not just reimbursement for a few investors in two of the failed schemes, Hajdari said.
He told students last November to wake up and put pressure on the right-wing Democratic Party government if they wanted to improve their conditions.
Hajdari is now leader of an independent trade union, with an estimated 130,000 members across the country.
